survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 student ratings aggregated to the school level via two-level CFA/SEM in Mplus. The paper reports the PISA sampling design as a two-stage stratified procedure (schools sampled first, then 15-year-old students within schools), but it does not report whether PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the Mplus estimation. Because the analysis is based on multilevel CFA/SEM (robust maximum likelihood) rather than predictive ML, the manuscript does not document any explicit weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife). Therefore, weighting strategy cannot be confirmed from the text; readers should verify in the original PISA technical documentation or the authors’ Mplus input files whether complex-survey weights were used.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this study are latent teaching-quality factors and intrinsic motivation measured by questionnaire items, analyzed via multilevel CFA/SEM. Plausible values are typically used for cognitive achievement scales in PISA, but this paper does not model PV-based achievement outcomes, so PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript does not report any missing-data handling strategy for the item responses used in the CFA/SEM (e.g., full-information maximum likelihood, listwise deletion, or multiple imputation), which is a reporting gap because missingness in survey items can affect factor estimation and reliability/validity indices.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the full available PISA 2015 student sample for all participating countries/regions (and additional regions such as Spain regions and Argentina Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos) as listed in the PISA 2015 database. The study does not report additional student-level exclusions beyond the standard PISA sampling procedure; it aggregates student ratings to the school level and estimates two-level CFA/SEM models per scale and per country/region. For some country/regions, model estimation failed to converge (reported as NC) or data were unavailable (NA), but no further explicit filtering criteria are described.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Science (15-year-olds) — classroom management scale (school-level aggregation)
main_findings.target_variable: Classroom management teaching quality (school-level latent factor)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Reliability (across countries): mean ICC-1=0.12 (SD=0.05), mean ICC-2=0.76 (SD=0.09). Predictive validity: average regression coefficient with intrinsic motivation=0.58 (SD=0.20); predictive in 86.2% of regions/countries (p<0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science the study estimated a two-level latent classroom management factor at the school level and evaluated its reliability and predictive validity for intrinsic motivation, finding that classroom management showed high school-level reliability (ICC-1≈0.12; ICC-2≈0.76) and positive predictive validity (average beta≈0.58, significant in most regions). This indicates that student ratings of classroom management can be used as a reasonably reliable school-level indicator of teaching quality in many countries/regions, supporting cautious use for school-level monitoring and research.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Science (15-year-olds) — emotional support scale (school-level aggregation)
main_findings.target_variable: Emotional support teaching quality (school-level latent factor)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Reliability (across countries): mean ICC-1=0.08 (SD=0.03), mean ICC-2=0.65 (SD=0.14). Predictive validity: average regression coefficient with intrinsic motivation=0.30 (SD=0.39); predictive in 45.9% of regions/countries (p<0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science the study estimated a two-level latent emotional support factor at the school level and evaluated its reliability and predictive validity for intrinsic motivation, finding that emotional support had low-to-marginal school-level reliability (ICC-1≈0.08; ICC-2≈0.65) and only moderate predictive validity (average beta≈0.30, significant in about half of regions). This indicates that emotional support ratings may be useful for school-level comparisons in some contexts but require checking country-specific reliability before policy or accountability use.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Science (15-year-olds) — adaptive instruction scale (school-level aggregation)
main_findings.target_variable: Adaptive instruction teaching quality (school-level latent factor)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Reliability (across countries): mean ICC-1=0.06 (SD=0.02), mean ICC-2=0.58 (SD=0.12). Predictive validity: average regression coefficient with intrinsic motivation=0.55 (SD=0.36); predictive in 63.5% of regions/countries (p<0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science the study estimated a two-level latent adaptive instruction factor at the school level and evaluated its reliability and predictive validity for intrinsic motivation, finding that adaptive instruction showed low school-level reliability on average (ICC-1≈0.06; ICC-2≈0.58) but still demonstrated positive predictive validity in many regions (average beta≈0.55; significant in 63.5%). This indicates that adaptive instruction ratings can reflect meaningful between-school differences for research and some policy targeting, but reliability thresholds should be verified per country/region.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Science (15-year-olds) — teacher-directed instruction scale (school-level aggregation)
main_findings.target_variable: Teacher-directed instruction teaching quality (school-level latent factor)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Reliability (across countries): mean ICC-1=0.08 (SD=0.06), mean ICC-2=0.64 (SD=0.16). Predictive validity: average regression coefficient with intrinsic motivation=0.69 (SD=0.28); predictive in 79.6% of regions/countries (p<0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science the study estimated a two-level latent teacher-directed instruction factor at the school level and evaluated its reliability and predictive validity for intrinsic motivation, finding that teacher-directed instruction had low-to-marginal school-level reliability on average (ICC-1≈0.08; ICC-2≈0.64) but strong predictive validity (average beta≈0.69; significant in 79.6% of regions). This indicates that teacher-directed instruction ratings can capture meaningful between-school teaching differences even when reliability is not uniformly high, suggesting targeted use with country-specific reliability checks.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Science (15-year-olds) — personal feedback scale (school-level aggregation)
main_findings.target_variable: Personal feedback teaching quality (school-level latent factor)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Reliability (across countries): mean ICC-1=0.07 (SD=0.04), mean ICC-2=0.62 (SD=0.15). Predictive validity: average regression coefficient with intrinsic motivation=-0.06 (SD=0.50); predictive in 19.0% of regions/countries (p<0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science the study estimated a two-level latent personal feedback factor at the school level and evaluated its reliability and predictive validity for intrinsic motivation, finding that personal feedback had marginal school-level reliability (ICC-1≈0.07; ICC-2≈0.62) and essentially no predictive validity on average (average beta≈-0.06; significant in only 19% of regions). This indicates that personal feedback items are likely better interpreted as student-level experiences rather than school-level teaching quality, limiting their use for school comparisons.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Science (15-year-olds) — inquiry-based instruction scale (school-level aggregation)
main_findings.target_variable: Inquiry-based instruction teaching quality (school-level latent factor)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Reliability (across countries): mean ICC-1=0.05 (SD=0.07), mean ICC-2=0.41 (SD=0.29). Predictive validity: average regression coefficient with intrinsic motivation=-0.08 (SD=0.51); predictive in 17.8% of regions/countries (p<0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science the study estimated a two-level latent inquiry-based instruction factor at the school level and evaluated its reliability and predictive validity for intrinsic motivation, finding that inquiry-based instruction had the weakest school-level reliability (ICC-1≈0.05; ICC-2≈0.41) and near-zero predictive validity on average (average beta≈-0.08; significant in 17.8% of regions). This indicates that inquiry-based instruction ratings in PISA 2015 are not well suited for school-level teaching quality measurement, and policy/research should avoid using this scale for school comparisons without further scale refinement.

data.outcome_summary: This study evaluates whether PISA 2015 science teaching scales—aggregated from students to the school level—yield reliable and valid measures of school-level teaching quality. Using multilevel CFA/SEM in Mplus (robust maximum likelihood), the authors estimated two-level unidimensional factor structures for six teaching scales and computed school-level reliability via ICC-1 and ICC-2, plus predictive validity by regressing school-level teaching factors on school-level intrinsic motivation. Across 69 countries/regions (503,146 students; 17,678 schools), classroom management showed the strongest school-level reliability (mean ICC-1=0.12; ICC-2=0.76) and positive predictive validity (average beta=0.58; significant in 86.2% of regions). Emotional support, adaptive instruction, and teacher-directed instruction showed low-to-marginal reliability but meaningful predictive validity in many regions, whereas personal feedback and inquiry-based instruction showed weak or inconsistent predictive validity. The paper does not report missing-data handling and does not document whether PISA complex-survey weights were applied, so results should be interpreted with caution for cross-country policy use.
